title: Category A (Arch)
disclaimer: This deck is a study aid for practicing recall of Category A ground school material. It is not a substitute for training from a certified USPA instructor or for the current official USPA Skydiver's Information Manual (SIM). Always verify procedures with your instructor and the current SIM.

cards.front: What three handles are on a student rig, and what does each one do?
cards.back:
• Main deployment handle: opens the main parachute
• Cutaway handle: releases the main parachute in an emergency
• Reserve handle: deploys the reserve parachute

cards.front: What are the three stages a parachute goes through when it opens?
cards.back:
• Activation: throwing the pilot chute, pulling the ripcord, or via static line
• Deployment: the parachute leaves the container
• Inflation: the canopy fills with air

cards.front: What does the reserve static line (RSL) do, and can you rely on it instead of pulling your handles?
cards.back: It connects the main risers to the reserve pin, so cutting away the main automatically starts reserve deployment. It's a backup only. Pulling your own handles in a malfunction is always your job.

cards.front: What does an automatic activation device (AAD) do, and is it something you can count on instead of pulling?
cards.back: It initiates reserve deployment at a preset altitude and speed. Like the RSL, it's strictly a backup device. You must still pull your own handles.

cards.front: When should you check your altimeter in freefall?
cards.back:
USPA SIM: Every 3 seconds.
Jumptown procedure: Every 5 seconds.
Also check after every maneuver or unexpected event.

cards.front: How many times will your instructor check your equipment on a Category A jump day?
cards.back:
Four times:
• Before you put the rig on
• Immediately after putting it on
• Before boarding the aircraft
• Again in the aircraft shortly before exit

cards.front: What altitude do AFF students initiate deployment at?
cards.back: 5,500 feet.

cards.front: How should you approach a fixed wing aircraft on the ground, and who should you be with?
cards.back: Approach from the rear, away from the propeller, and always accompanied by your instructor.

cards.front: Who's responsible for making sure you're wearing your seatbelt or restraint during taxi, takeoff, and landing?
cards.back: Both the pilot and the jumper share that responsibility under FAA regulations.

cards.front: What's your very first response if the aircraft has an emergency?
cards.back: Stay calm and wait for a command from your instructor.

cards.front: What four actions might your instructor direct you to take in an aircraft emergency?
cards.back:
• Land in the aircraft
• Exit and use your reserve
• Exit and use your main
• Perform a routine exit (with or without instructor assistance)

cards.front: If you're told to land with the aircraft during an emergency, what should you do?
cards.back:
• Make sure your helmet and seatbelt/restraint are secure
• Take the safety position your instructor taught you
• Clasp your hands behind your head to reinforce your neck
• After landing, unfasten your restraint and exit promptly, walking at least 100 feet from the plane

cards.front: If you exit the aircraft during an emergency, what should you do?
cards.back:
• Get your parachute open immediately
• Look for your instructor's canopy and follow it to a clear area (or pick any clear area if you can't find them)
• Prepare for a PLF

cards.front: A parachute opens accidentally inside the aircraft. What should you do?
cards.back:
Try to contain it and tell your instructor.
• If your parachute goes out the door, follow it out immediately
• If it's someone else's parachute going out the door, push them out through the door right away too

Both actions prevent injury or damage to the plane.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a good exit?
cards.back:
• Setup
• Launch
• Flyaway (the transition to belly to earth flight is also called "the hill")

cards.front: What's the AFF check in sequence right before you exit?
cards.back:
• Call "Check in!" to the inside instructor, who responds "OK!"
• Call "Check out!" to the outside instructor, who responds "OK!"
• Begin a count such as "Up, down, arch!" or "Out, in, arch!"

At Jumptown, the count is "Prop, up, down, step out, arch!"

cards.front: As an AFF student, what should you do if you're unstable right after exit?
cards.back:
• Check your altitude
• Arch until the horizon comes flat into view
• Follow your instructors' signals
• If you lose one instructor, continue as usual
• If you lose both, pull immediately

cards.front: What are the key elements of a neutral, arched body position?
cards.back:
• Hips forward with back arched
• Knees about shoulder width apart
• Legs extended slightly, knees bent 45 degrees, toes pointed
• Upper arms 90 degrees or less from the torso and relaxed
• Elbows bent 90 to 120 degrees
• Chin up

cards.front: What three things does a "circle of awareness" check?
cards.back:
• Heading: Look at the horizon
• Altitude: Check the altimeter
• Instructors: Look to them for signals. Check the reserve side instructor first, then the main side instructor.

cards.front: What does HAALR stand for, and when do you use it?
cards.back:
• Heading (look at the horizon)
• Altitude (most important)
• Arch (hips forward, chin up)
• Legs (ensure neutral leg position)
• Relax (take a deep breath)

This is the checklist you cycle through for the rest of an AFF freefall after your second circle of awareness.

cards.front: At what altitude do you lock on to your altimeter, and at what altitude do you wave off (AFF)?
cards.back:
• Lock on at 6,000 feet and keep watching until you see 5,500 feet
• Wave off at 5,500 feet

cards.front: What's the AFF deployment sequence once you reach your pull altitude?
cards.back:
• Wave off (both arms overhead)
• Arch
• Reach
• Pull

cards.front: What are your three pull priorities, in order?
cards.back:
• Pull
• Pull at altitude
• Pull, preferably while stable

Altitude always takes priority over stability.

cards.front: You're on your back at pull altitude. What do you do?
cards.back: Pull. Pulling at the correct altitude matters more than pulling in a stable position.

cards.front: You see your instructor pull. What should you do?
cards.back: Pull.

cards.front: After you pull, what should you do while waiting to confirm the canopy is deploying?
cards.back:
• Return both hands to the neutral arch position
• Remain arched and stable with your shoulders level
• Count to 3 (5 for Jumptown) by 1,000's
• Visually check for pilot chute and main canopy deployment

cards.front: You can't find your main deployment handle. What's the procedure?
cards.back:
• Feel across the bottom of the container to the corner, then down the side to the corner
• No more than two tries or 5 seconds, whichever comes first
• If you still can't find it, start emergency procedures

cards.front: You find the handle but it won't pull (a "hard pull"). What do you do?
cards.back:
• Try to throw the pilot chute (no more than two tries or 5 seconds)
• If that doesn't work, start emergency procedures

cards.front: Your pilot chute is stuck in the burble behind your back. How do you clear it?
cards.back:
• Twist at the waist and look over your shoulder to change the airflow (no more than two tries or 5 seconds)
• If it still won't launch off your back, start emergency procedures

cards.front: The pilot chute's bridle wraps around your arm or leg. What do you do?
cards.back:
• Arch harder for stability
• Point the entangled limb up at the sky to try to shake it free (no more than two tries or 5 seconds)
• If it doesn't clear, start emergency procedures

cards.front: Your container opens prematurely in freefall. What's the procedure?
cards.back:
• Try to locate and deploy the pilot chute (no more than two tries or 5 seconds)
• If you can't, cut away and deploy the reserve

cards.front: With both toggles all the way up, how does the canopy fly? What happens when you pull one toggle down?
cards.back:
That's full flight, straight ahead at full speed.
• A small toggle pull gives a gentle turn
• A bigger pull gives a faster, diving turn

cards.front: What are the three canopy check questions you ask right after opening?
cards.back:
"Is it there? Is it square? Is it steerable?"

At Jumptown, this is taught as four words: "there / square / stable / steerable."

cards.front: What does "square" mean when checking your canopy?
cards.back:
• Four well defined edges forming a rectangular shape
• Suspension lines cascading down in four neat groups to the risers
• Slider down to the tops of the risers
• Flying level and stable, not turning or spinning

cards.front: How do you perform the steerability part of your canopy check?
cards.back:
• Unstow your toggles and confirm straight flight
• Flare fully and smoothly return to full flight to check braking
• Turn right at least 90 degrees, then return to full flight
• Turn left at least 90 degrees, then return to full flight

cards.front: What is "decision altitude" for a student, and what does it mean?
cards.back: 2,500 feet: the lowest altitude by which you must decide whether your canopy is safe to land. If it's not, you must immediately start emergency procedures.

cards.front: You have line twists after opening. What's the priority?
cards.back:
Clear line twists first, before addressing anything else:
• Spread the risers and kick
• Release the brakes only after the twists are cleared

cards.front: Besides line twists, what other minor canopy opening problems might you see, and how do you usually fix them?
cards.back:
• End cells that stay closed
• A slider that stays up near the canopy
• An unintended turn

Unlike line twists, you can usually solve these with a canopy control check.

If the problem continues or gets worse, initiate your emergency procedures by 2,500 feet. If in doubt, initiate your emergency procedures.

cards.front: What is the "cutaway hard deck," and what do you do below it?
cards.back: 1,000 feet: below this altitude it's too low to safely cut away. Instead, you deploy the reserve and land both canopies.

cards.front: Above your hard deck, what's the malfunction procedure?
cards.back:
• Confirm you're above 1,000 feet
• Cut away
• Pull your reserve

cards.front: You have a biplane (two canopies out) situation. What do you do?
cards.back:
Land both canopies.
• Leave toggles stowed unless the toggles on one canopy are already unstowed (then unstow the other)
• Gently steer the front canopy using its rear risers
• Land without flaring and perform a PLF

cards.front: You have a side by side (two canopies out) situation. What do you do?
cards.back:
Land both canopies.
• Leave toggles stowed unless the toggles on one canopy are already unstowed (then unstow the other)
• Gently steer whichever canopy is more directly overhead, using its rear risers
• Land without flaring and perform a PLF

cards.front: You have a downplane. What makes this malfunction different, and what must you do?
cards.back: You must cut away regardless of altitude. This is the only exception to the cutaway hard deck rule at 1,000 feet.

cards.front: What should you do in a main/reserve entanglement?
cards.back:
Land both canopies.
• Never give up trying to clear the entanglement or get the parachutes to inflate
• Do your best to fly straight for landing and perform a PLF

cards.front: After confirming you have a good canopy, what should you do next, and by what altitude should you reach your holding area?
cards.back:
• Check your altitude and locate the airport and holding area
• Arrive at or above 2,000 feet to be positioned to enter your landing pattern correctly

cards.front: How should you respond to canopy traffic and a potential collision?
cards.back:
• Regularly check APT: Altitude, Position, Traffic throughout canopy flight
• If a collision is imminent, both jumpers should generally steer right
• If you collide and become entangled, communicate your intentions before acting
• If you remain entangled below 1,000 feet and the canopies are uncontrollable, both jumpers deploy their reserves

cards.front: What are the three legs of a standard landing pattern, and around what altitudes do they start?
cards.back:
• Downwind: starts around 900 feet, at the pattern entry point
• Base: around 600 feet
• Final: around 300 feet

cards.front: What are your landing priorities, in order?
cards.back:
• Land with a level wing
• Land in a clear, open area
• Flare and perform a PLF

cards.front: Is landing into the wind one of your official landing priorities?
cards.back: No. It's desirable, but it is not one of the actual landing priorities.

cards.front: If you realize you're going to land downwind, what should you do?
cards.back: Continue straight with a level wing, flare normally, and prepare for a PLF instead of attempting a low turn to correct into the wind. Low turns close to the ground are dangerous.

cards.front: When should you start your flare, and when should you finish it?
cards.back:
• Start when your feet are roughly twice your height above the ground
• Finish (toggles all the way down) when your feet are about one to three feet above the ground

cards.front: What happens if you let the toggles back up abruptly after starting your flare?
cards.back: It causes a steep dive toward the ground, known as a "flight cycle." Once you start a flare you can stop and hold, but you can't undo it and start over.

cards.front: What's the correct PLF (parachute landing fall) sequence?
cards.back:
Feet touch down first, then roll:
• Balls of the feet
• To the calf
• To the thigh
• Through the small of the back
• Diagonally across to the opposite shoulder, continuing to roll to spread out the impact

cards.front: By what altitude should you decide whether you need an alternate landing area?
cards.back:
By 2,000 feet, decide whether you can reach the pattern entry point at 900 feet:
• If not, aim for the point at 600 feet or 300 feet that you can reach
• If none are reachable, plan to land in the nearest open, obstacle free area (which might even be behind you)

cards.front: When is it easiest to spot ground obstacles before landing?
cards.back: During the downwind leg, since you're closer to the ground.

cards.front: What's the procedure for landing in water?
cards.back:
• Flare and PLF in case it's shallow
• After landing, try to stand up
• If you can't touch bottom, swim out of your gear and leave it behind

cards.front: What's the procedure for landing in trees?
cards.back:
• Keep your arms close and legs together
• Use a half flare entering the tree
• Be ready to finish your flare and PLF if you drop to the ground
• If you end up suspended, hold on, wait for help, and don't try to climb down

cards.front: You're landing on a rooftop. What's the procedure?
cards.back:
• Flare and PLF
• Disconnect the RSL if you can and cut away
• Wait for help, and don't attempt to climb down

cards.front: You're headed into the side of a building. What should you do?
cards.back:
• Preparing: Prepare for a PLF, and turn the canopy slightly to strike a glancing blow
• Landing: Half flare, then PLF against the building
• After: As you drop to the ground, finish the flare and PLF

cards.front: What's the procedure for landing near or in power lines?
cards.back:
• Drop any handles
• Flare and PLF, touching no more than one wire at a time
• Your parachute can conduct electricity. If suspended in the wires, do NOT cut away; wait for qualified personnel to confirm the power is off
• If your feet reach the ground, disconnect the RSL and cut away, leaving the main behind

cards.front: What's the complete AFF dive flow, from exit to canopy check?
cards.back:
• Safe exit
• Circle of awareness (COA)
• Three practice deployments
• Second circle of awareness (COA)
• HAALR
• 6,000 feet: lock on
• 5,500 feet: wave off and pull
• Canopy check: APT
